items.title: 56800_John Simmons oral history interview
items.q: So the Sister out there, name was Sister Bonneville, she suggested that I chew chewing gum for my nerves.

ctx.x: A long period of time of smoking, combined with nerves. Nerves goes along with it. You can't have emphysema without being nervous, no, no. And then there's people that get emphysema without smoking, just by being exposed to a lot of smoke, you know, over a period of time. Now, like I started smoking when I was 12 years old. I was sniffing and smoking. Then I had an appendectomy, a ruptured appendectomy, it wasn't ruptured. I'm sorry. It was--my appendix had formed a -- a corruption had formed over my appendix,…

inwardly, you know. I couldn't straighten up, from this appendix thing hurting me so. And when he straightened me up, I fainted right there on the floor. And it started, this thing, to leak, and the Catholics sent me to St. John's Hospital over there in Tulsa, Oklahoma, where they didn't receive any blacks. There was only three blacks there the whole time I was there. One was a basketball player from a little town called Bartlesville. He was a good basketball player, but he got both feet broke. The way the…

in 1930, slipping out smoking. Then '34, New Years Day, they had me on the operating table, in '34. I stayed in the hospital, I guess, about six months. They made this incision, and they inserted a bicycle tube in there, for it to drain out. Well, at that time they didn't have penicillin or any myecin drugs or sulfadrug. They didn't have anything like that. So I'm lucky to be here now, you know, for what they had to work with at that time. And instead of this corruption coming out of this incision, it passed by…
